I have farmed these alluvial soils of Quzhou County on the North China Plain for more than forty years, and at sixty-seven I see no reason to gamble on crops I do not know inside and out. The wheat–maize double-cropping rotation has always put food on my table and cash in my pocket, so this year I will stick to it. I will manage twelve mu of improved winter wheat that is already in the ground from last autumn’s sowing, and I will follow it on the same land with twelve mu of hybrid summer maize planted directly after the June harvest. Because I finished high school, I can read pesticide labels and follow extension bulletins, but I am also old enough to trust experience over fads. I will rotary-till the wheat plots and apply four irrigations and about four pesticide sprays through the spring to protect the crop from insects, weeds, and fungus. For the maize I will use no-tillage direct seeding to save my back and keep soil moisture during the hot summer, with two irrigations and three pesticide applications. My fertilizer rates are moderate—enough to keep yields high without throwing money away.
